Why don't you just use a LiveUSB and dd to create a compressed backup?

To backup your HD, boot into a LiveUSB and plug in your portable drive, then find your disks with lsblk. You should see something like this:

NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
sda 8:0 0 500G 0 disk 
|-sda1 8:1 0 200M 0 part /boot
`-sda2 8:2 0 480G 0 part /
sdb 8:16 1 14.5G 0 disk 
sdc 8:0 0 700G 0 disk 
`-sdc1 8:2 0 700G 0 part ext4

Yours may not look EXACTLY like this, but it will be similar. You can see that there is a parent partition table for your HD, which says it's 500G (or close to it), which is /dev/sda. Both sda1 and sda2 are "child" partitions, and you will have a couple of extra partitions for Windows... don't worry about all the child partitions, just worry about that parent partition table, /dev/sda. This will be the notation I use here.

You'll also need to take note of your portable drive, which is /dev/sdc in this example, given by the 700G size. Yours may not be sdc, but it'll definitely be sd-something, and I will be using /dev/sdc in my examples. In my example, it has nothing under MOUNTPOINT and needs to be mounted. If you don't know how to do that, you can do it with:

sudo mount /dev/sdc1 /mnt

which will mount it to the /mnt directory. I will be using this directory in my examples.

You'll also notice a smaller /dev/sdb which should be your LiveUSB. This isn't important, and you can just ignore it.

Once you have all that information, run this:

sudo dd status=progress bs=4M if=/dev/sda | gzip > /mnt/backup_image.gz

where /dev/sda is your HD, mnt is where you mounted your portable drive, and backup_image is whatever you want to name your compressed .gz backup image.

Then, when you want to restore the image, just run:

sudo gzip -dc /mnt/backup_image.gz | dd status=progress bs=4M of=/dev/sda

again, with /dev/sda being your HD, mnt being the path to your portable drive, and backup_image.gz being the compressed image you took in the first part. It will decompress your backup, and restore it to your HD.

These processes will take a bit-for-bit image of your HD, and back it up -- or restore it -- for you. Since we used the "parent" partition /dev/sda as an input, it will back up all of the child partitions, including both of your Windows and Linux OS's. And, since we're also compressing it, you should have space on your portable drive for a couple of backups.
